title: Highest-weight classification and contragredients of simple rational modules
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure] and let $G$ be a semisimple $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], meaning smooth, connected, affine and of finite type with no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup; solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes become trivial. A rational $G$-module is an $F$-vector space $V$ with a coaction $V\to V\otimes_F F[G]$ satisfying coassociativity and the counit identity. A submodule is a linear subspace whose coaction takes values in its tensor product with $F[G]$. Simple means nonzero with no proper nonzero submodule. Equivariance means a coaction identity, equivalently equivariance after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq G$ and a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$ with unipotent radical $U$, character lattice $X=X^*(T)$ and positive roots $\Phi^+$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Choose a longest Weyl element $w_0$, which sends $\Phi^+$ onto $-\Phi^+$; its action on $X$ is $(w\lambda)(t)=\lambda(n^{-1}tn)$ for a normalizer representative $n$. For every finite-dimensional simple rational $G$-module $V$, the subspace $V^U=\{v:\rho_V(v)|_U=v\otimes1\}$ is one-dimensional, and $T$ acts on it by a character $\lambda(V)\in X$, called its highest weight. The contragredient $V^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_F(V,F)$, with $(g\ell)(v)=\ell(g^{-1}v)$ after every scalar extension, is simple and satisfies $\lambda(V^\vee)=-w_0\lambda(V)$. Two finite-dimensional simple rational $G$-modules with the same highest weight are equivariantly linearly isomorphic.

proof.text: Write $Q_+=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}\mathbf N\alpha$ and $\mu\le\nu$ when $\nu-\mu\in Q_+$. The simple-root base in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] is linearly independent, so $Q_+\cap(-Q_+)=\{0\}$ and this order is antisymmetric. For any finite-dimensional rational $T$-module, choose $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$ and apply [lem-sfb-gm-representation-weight-basis] to the first factor, then each subsequent factor on the preceding weight spaces; the factor actions commute and hence preserve these spaces. This gives the finite direct sum of character spaces. More explicitly, the coaction in Laurent monomials is $c(x)=\sum_a x_a\otimes t^a$; coassociativity and the counit give $c(x_a)=x_a\otimes t^a$ and $x=\sum_a x_a$. Comparing coefficients also shows that every $T$-stable subspace contains all weight components of its vectors. These observations apply to invariant subspaces, quotients and duals as well.

source.place: Theorem 12.12 and Remark 12.13, printed pp.234–235; root order preceding 22.2, printed p.463

proof.text: The Borel-pair node gives $B=U\rtimes T$ with $U$ smooth connected unipotent. By its unipotence hypothesis there is a faithful finite-dimensional representation of $U$ in which all geometric points are unipotent. Choose bases for this representation and for the nonzero $V$. Apply [lem-sfb-unipotent-rational-representation-fixed-vector] to the restriction of $V$ to $U$, and then [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-invariant-descent] with $k=K=F$. Thus $V^U\ne0$ for the coaction notion of invariants. Normality of $U$ in $B$ makes $V^U$ $T$-stable: $u(tv)=t(t^{-1}ut)v=tv$, as an identity after every scalar extension. The weight decomposition of step 1 therefore supplies $0\ne v\in(V^U)_\lambda$. Since every $b$ is $ut$, this line has $B$-character $\lambda\circ p$.

The dual is rational: in a basis its action matrix is the inverse transpose of the action matrix of $V$; inversion is supplied by the antipode of $F[G]$. For a rational submodule $0\ne W\subsetneq V^\vee$, its annihilator $W^\perp\subset V$ has dimension $\dim V-\dim W$, strictly between $0$ and $\dim V$. It is $G$-stable, since for every test algebra $A$, $g\in G(A)$, $x\in W^\perp\otimes A$ and $\ell\in W\otimes A$ one has $\ell(gx)=(g^{-1}\ell)(x)=0$. Annihilators commute with extension to $A$ by choosing an adapted basis of the finite-dimensional vector space. This contradicts simplicity of $V$. Also $\dim V^\vee=\dim V>0$. Thus $V^\vee$ is simple, and steps 1–3 apply to it.

source.place: The highest weight of the contragredient representation, printed p.471: simplicity of the dual, with the annihilator argument written out

proof.text: If $n\in N_G(T)(F)$ represents $w$, then $t(nx)=n(n^{-1}tn)x=(w\mu)(t)nx$ for $x\in V_\mu$, after every scalar extension. The maps $n,n^{-1}$ therefore identify $V_\mu$ with $V_{w\mu}$, so the finite set of weights is Weyl invariant. Since every weight $\mu\le\lambda$, and $w_0$ sends every positive root to a negative root, $w_0\mu-w_0\lambda\in Q_+$. Every weight is $w_0\mu$ for some weight $\mu$, so $w_0\lambda$ is the least weight of $V$, and it occurs. The weight decomposition of step 1 identifies the weights of $V^\vee$ with the negatives of those of $V$: the dual of $V_\mu$ has character $-\mu$. Thus $-w_0\lambda$ occurs and dominates every dual weight. By step 3 for the simple $V^\vee$, its highest weight also occurs and dominates every dual weight. Antisymmetry gives $\lambda(V^\vee)=-w_0\lambda$.

source.place: Lemma 22.15, printed pp.466–467, and The highest weight of the contragredient representation, printed p.471

proof.text: Finally, suppose $V_1,V_2$ are simple with highest weight $\lambda$, and choose nonzero highest vectors $v_1,v_2$ using steps 1–3. In $V_1\oplus V_2$, let $C$ be the rational submodule generated by $v=(v_1,v_2)$. This is a $B$-eigenvector of weight $\lambda$. The cyclic weight bound gives $C_\lambda=F(v_1,v_2)$. Each projection $p_i:C\to V_i$ is equivariant and has nonzero image, hence is surjective. The kernel of $p_2$ is $C\cap(V_1\oplus0)$, a submodule of the simple $V_1\oplus0$. It cannot be all of that module: otherwise $(v_1,0)\in C_\lambda=F(v_1,v_2)$, impossible since both $v_i\ne0$. Hence the kernel is zero. The same argument interchanging 1 and 2 proves $p_1$ bijective. The map $p_2p_1^{-1}:V_1\to V_2$ is the required equivariant linear isomorphism; the inverse of a bijective coaction-compatible linear map is coaction-compatible by composing its coaction identity with its linear inverse.

The canonical dual coaction is existentially asserted with its full antipode contraction characterization, which uniquely determines it; no arbitrary dual representation or chosen data is used.
